title: Engineer the Value

lessons.title: Design an offer that attracts interest while reducing resistance
body: A customer can want the result your product promises and still hesitate — because they doubt it will actually work, expect to wait too long for it to pay off, or believe it will take too much effort. The Pull/Drag Map examines both sides of that hesitation at once: what pulls the customer toward your offer, and what drags against them taking action. It splits that into four forces — two that create attraction, two that create resistance.

Outcome Pull — how desirable is the result?
An outcome pulls harder when it's specific and meaningful, not broad and vague — a vague promise asks the customer to imagine their own version of success, while a specific one hands them a picture they can see themselves reaching. This is also the difference between selling a feature and communicating a result: “12 video lessons” is a feature; “you'll finally understand why your last three posts flopped” is a result. To make an outcome more specific, work from what the customer actually said they wanted in Module 2's research, not from what your product technically does:
WEAKER
“Improve your social media.”
STRONGER
“Plan a full week of useful social media content without starting from a blank page every day.”
The second version pulls harder because it names the specific pain (the blank page), the specific win (a week planned in one sitting) and leaves nothing for the customer to guess. If you can't picture a specific customer reading your outcome statement and nodding, it's still too vague.

Proof Pull — how confident can the customer feel it'll work?
Desire alone doesn't close a sale — customers hesitate the moment they can't imagine the solution working for someone like them. Proof closes that gap: demonstrations, before/after previews, worked examples, testimonials, case studies and plainly transparent explanations of the method all give the customer something concrete to believe. A brand-new creator with no testimonials yet isn't stuck — showing your own worked example or simply being transparent about how the process works can build real credibility before a single review exists. What doesn't build credibility is an unsupported guarantee or an exaggerated claim; customers discount those automatically, and an obviously inflated promise reduces trust rather than raising it.

Speed Drag — how long does the customer expect to wait?
Resistance builds the longer a customer expects to wait before feeling any benefit — and it's their perception of waiting time that matters, not the literal time to finish the whole product. The fix isn't promising instant transformation; that's not acceptable, and customers have learned to distrust it. The fix is shortening the time to a first, real result: a structured milestone, a quick win in session one, ready-made resources that remove setup time, or simply a shorter path to the first visible outcome. A social-media content product might promise a full week of content planned in a single 45-minute sitting — not “mastering content strategy,” which sounds like a long project, but a specific, fast first win.

Effort Drag — how much work or sacrifice does it ask of them?
Complexity and decision fatigue create resistance on their own, independent of how long something takes — a process can be quick and still feel exhausting if it forces too many decisions along the way. Every extra step or unclear instruction is a small chance for someone to put the product down and not come back. Templates, checklists, pre-built resources, filled-in examples and guided, one-decision-at-a-time workflows all reduce this — a done-for-you caption template the customer fills in, rather than writes from scratch. Reducing effort does not mean removing learning or practice the customer genuinely needs; it means removing friction that has nothing to do with that learning.

How to strengthen your offer
Diagnosing a weak force only helps if you know what to do about it:
ForceWhat a weak score might indicatePractical improvement
Outcome PullThe result is vague or unimportant.Make the outcome more specific and relevant.
Proof PullThe customer can't see why the solution should work.Add demonstrations, previews, examples or credible evidence.
Speed DragThe customer expects a long wait before experiencing value.Introduce quick wins, milestones and ready-to-use resources.
Effort DragThe customer expects too much work or complexity.Simplify the process, provide templates and remove unnecessary steps.
None of these are one-line fixes — each changes something real about the product. For a social-media content product: a weak Outcome Pull might mean rewriting the sales page around “a week of content planned in one sitting” instead of “better social media.” A weak Proof Pull might mean recording yourself actually planning a week of content live, so the customer watches the method work before buying. A weak Speed Drag often means restructuring delivery, not the content — splitting one long course into “session one: leave with next week's content already planned.” A weak Effort Drag usually means building the templates you'd otherwise expect the customer to build — a caption swipe file instead of a blank page.

How to score honestly
The exercise below asks you to rate all four forces from 1 to 10. As a practical guide — not a scientifically validated threshold — 1–3 represents a weak force, 4–7 a moderate or developing one, and 8–10 a strong one. What “strong” means isn't the same on both axes: for Outcome Pull and Proof Pull, higher is generally favourable. For Speed Drag and Effort Drag, higher means more resistance, so higher is generally unfavourable. Don't treat all four sliders as if a high number is always good — a 9 on Effort Drag is a warning, not an achievement.
A WORKED EXAMPLE — HYPOTHETICAL
A hypothetical small business owner is building a product that helps other small business owners plan and produce social media content.
Outcome Pull: 8 — the result is specific and addresses a real, recognisable frustration.
Proof Pull: 4 — no demonstration yet of the method working, so a new customer has to take it on faith.
Speed Drag: 6 — one session produces a plan, but there's no “first win in ten minutes” moment yet.
Effort Drag: 7 — the customer still writes every caption and chooses every design themselves.
These are illustrative judgments about a hypothetical product, not market research or verified customer feedback. Reading this set: Outcome Pull is genuinely strong, so it isn't holding this offer back. Of the remaining three, Effort Drag at 7 sits closest to becoming a real problem — and templates are a more direct fix than rebuilding trust from scratch. The creator should improve Effort Drag first, then come back to Proof Pull — not because Proof Pull doesn't matter, but because removing the bigger obstacle first matters more.

Reading the four zones
Your average Pull score (Outcome Pull and Proof Pull) and average Drag score (Speed Drag and Effort Drag) place your offer in one of four zones — Pull increasing left to right, Drag increasing bottom to top:
  • Magnetic (high Pull, low Drag) — desirable and credible, with low perceived wait and effort. The zone to aim for — though landing here isn't proof the offer will sell, only that your own assessment is favourable.
  • Slow Burn (high Pull, high Drag) — customers want the result but anticipate real resistance. Usually fixed by reducing perceived wait or effort, not the outcome itself.
  • Mild Interest (low Pull, low Drag) — easy to try, but not compelling enough to bother. Points back to Outcome Pull or Proof Pull.
  • Hard Sell (low Pull, high Drag) — limited attraction and real resistance. Often the honest move is reworking the outcome before patching the resistance around it.
Whichever zone you land in, it's telling you where to look — not giving you a final verdict.

Working through the framework — hypothetical
Here's the same hypothetical small business owner moving through the framework end to end: define the outcome (a week of content planned in one sitting) → assess its attractiveness (strong — names a specific frustration from Module 2) → assess the evidence behind it (weak — no demonstration exists yet) → estimate the wait (moderate — a plan by the end of one session) → estimate the effort (moderate-to-high — captions and designs are still fully manual) → rate all four forces (8, 4, 6, 7) → interpret the zone (Pull averaging 6, Drag averaging 6.5 — closer to Slow Burn than Magnetic) → choose the weakest force to improve (Effort Drag, the cheapest real fix) → decide the change (a caption swipe file and a small set of post templates, so the customer edits rather than creates from nothing).The same process applies outside social media — a hypothetical fitness coach building a beginner home-workout plan might find Speed Drag is the weak force, since the program works but nothing feels different until week three, and fix it with a single “feel the difference” session in week one. None of this replaces real customer evidence; it's a way to examine your own judgment before you have that evidence, and to keep examining it as more comes in.

What this map can — and can't — tell you
The Pull/Drag Map is a diagnostic tool, not a prediction engine. It does not predict actual sales, and a strong-looking set of scores doesn't prove demand — it only reflects how convincing the offer looks to you right now. Where possible, base improvements on customer evidence from Modules 1 and 2 rather than on the score itself, and resist the urge to maximise every number — fixing the one force that's genuinely holding the offer back matters more than chasing a 10 on a force that's already strong.
lessons.insight: The objective is not to chase a perfect score. It's to identify what makes the offer less attractive or harder to adopt, then improve that one thing.

exercise.instructions: Rate your concept on all four forces, then write one sentence naming the outcome your customer wants.

prompt.title: Engineer the Value Prompt
prompt.purpose: Use this to pressure-test which force is actually holding your offer back.
prompt.template: You are an offer strategist using DigitalOps's Pull/Drag Map. My product concept: {{m2.summary}}. My outcome statement: {{m3.outcomeStatement}}. For each of the four forces — Outcome Pull, Proof Pull, Speed Drag, Effort Drag — tell me in plain language what would most increase it for this specific offer, then tell me which force looks weakest based on what I've described, explain in one or two sentences why that force looks weak, and flag anywhere your reasoning rests on an assumption about my offer rather than something I've actually told you. If my outcome statement is too vague to judge any force, say which part is vague and ask me to make it concrete before continuing. If my stated effort or time delay sounds optimistic compared to how this kind of work normally goes, say so. This is a judgment exercise, not a statistical one — don't present your answer as a validated score, and don't invent data about how long similar projects "normally" take beyond reasonable, stated common sense.
